title: Control Over Cost, Not Just Models — One-Page Narrative
content:
Context and goal:
This is a compact go-to-market narrative intended for engineers, platform teams, and technical buyers who already know models are valuable. They don’t need another model pitch — they need predictable economics, operational guarantees, and a clear migration path. Use this one-pager for sales briefs, partner decks, and internal alignment.

Core thesis (one sentence):
Teams win by owning predictable inference, not model ownership — Redwood delivers the control plane for latency, cost, and reliability across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments so engineering teams can ship consistent LLM-powered features without rebuilding infra.

Why this matters (the problem):
- Model quality is improving rapidly; the bottleneck for production adoption is serving economics and reliability.
- Teams are stuck between three unsatisfactory choices: public LLM APIs that are simple but unpredictable on cost/latency; self-hosted runtimes that require deep infra expertise and constant tuning; and cloud-managed endpoints that lack developer ergonomics or observability.
- Result: feature velocity slows, budgets spike unpredictably, and business risk increases.

Redwood’s positioning (3 core pillars):
1) Predictable economics and controls
   - Plain language: reduce variance in per-token cost and make it measurable and actionable.
   - How we deliver it: autoscaling policies + dedicated capacity, intelligent batching and KV/prefix caching, and quantization profiles recommended by workload.
   - Buyer benefit: finance and platform teams can forecast cost and avoid surprise bills.

2) Production-first developer experience
   - Plain language: same API and tooling whether you run in our hosted cloud, a reserved pool, or a customer VPC.
   - How we deliver it: compatible SDKs, seamless model pinning and rollouts (canary/A-B/fallback), and developer-friendly primitives (streaming, function calling, structured outputs).
   - Buyer benefit: teams iterate fast and ship features with predictable behavior in integration and testing.

3) Operational guarantees and graceful degradation
   - Plain language: keep customer-facing features available even when capacity or models fluctuate.
   - How we deliver it: smart routing, multi-variant fallback, regional failover, and SLA-backed latency for Dedicated customers.
   - Buyer benefit: reliability SLOs you can commit to without building complex cross-region logic.

Positioning statements (short, audience-targeted):
- For builders (engineering/ML eng): "Same API, fewer surprises — predictable latency and per-token economics so you can iterate on product, not infra."
- For platform teams: "Standardize inference across teams with pluggable capacity tiers and rollout controls that reduce variance across apps."
- For procurement/finance: "Forecastable consumption with reserved capacity and transparent unit economics — lower tail-risk on cloud AI spend."

Competitive frame (how we differ from the three poles):
- Compared to simple LLM APIs: we trade some initial setup for predictable cost, capacity controls, and enterprise-grade observability.
- Compared to self-hosted runtimes: we remove the day-two ops burden (kernel selection, KV caching, batching logic) and provide migration paths to on-prem or VPC with the same control plane.
- Compared to cloud managed endpoints: we emphasize developer ergonomics (SDK parity), model compatibility across environments, and explicit cost-savings levers.

Proof points & demo hooks (what to show in 10 minutes):
- Cost demo: show baseline per-token bill for a sample Q&A workload, then show optimizations applied (batching + cache + quantization profile) and the resulting % reduction in cost and latency changes.
- Reliability demo: show a canary rollout with automatic rollback to a fallback model under load.
- Observability: show token-level cost breakdown and a route-level latency heatmap in Console.

Common buyer objections and rebuttals: 
- "Why not just use OpenAPI/hosted LLMs?" -> "If you care about predictable economics and SLOs, hosted endpoints alone leave big gaps. We provide the controls and metrics you need to run at scale without reengineering."
- "Can’t we self-host and save money?" -> "Self-hosting hides significant ongoing ops cost and complexity. We combine production-grade runtime optimizations with operational tooling so your team focuses on product not kernel tuning."
- "What about model freshness and control?" -> "You can pin model versions, roll forward/back, and choose fallback variants; our catalog includes vetted open models and recommended quantization for each workload."

Tactical messaging dos and don’ts (for content & sales):
- DO lead with economics and reliability for technical buyers. Keep model talk secondary.
- DO use developer-centric language (SDK, rollout, tracing) when talking to engineers.
- DON’T overpromise raw model accuracy gains — promise predictable delivery and measurable unit economics.

Suggested top-of-funnel copy (3 variants):
1) Engineer-focused: "Ship features faster: a single inference API, predictable costs, and rollout controls that scale with your product."
2) Platform-focused: "Standardize inference across teams — predictable capacity, cost controls, and observability without lock-in."
3) Executive/finance: "Turn AI spend into a forecastable line item: reserved capacity, measurable unit economics, and SLA-backed reliability."

Next steps and experiments (90-day plan):
- Create a short benchmark playbook showing step-by-step how to reduce per-token costs on a representative chat workload (include scripts + Console screenshots).
- Build a 1-page sales enablement card for platform leads: key questions to qualify (SLOs, spend variance, regulatory needs).
- Run three pilot kits with existing mid-market accounts to capture measured delta on cost and latency pre/post Redwood.

Open questions for product/engineering to support messaging:
- Can we produce a canonical "cost delta" benchmark for three workload archetypes (chat, assistant, embeddings) that’s repeatable?
- What are the minimal observability snapshots sales can show in a live demo without provisioning Dedicated?

Quick internal CTA:
If you’re creating collateral or a demo targeted at builders or platform teams, start from the three pillars (economics, developer UX, reliability). Use the demo hooks above and route requests for benchmark assets to eng-applied-ml.

Author notes: drafted with input from Liam (field feedback) and Nora (product). This is intentionally short and modular — copy any sections into decks or one-pagers.
